lessons.title: Identifying Quality Coconuts in Your Area
lessons.body: When selecting coconuts for oil production, you want fruits that are mature and heavy with water. In most African coastal areas, coconuts are harvested year-round, but the best quality comes from trees that are at least 5 years old. Look for coconuts with a dry, brown husk and no cracks. Shake the coconut: if you hear liquid sloshing, it's fresh; if there's no sound, it's likely old and dried out. A good coconut should feel heavy for its sizeâaround 1.5 to 2 kg. Avoid coconuts with mold, soft spots, or a sour smell. For oil, you can use both mature and slightly immature nuts, but mature nuts yield more oil. In markets, ask the seller to cut one open for you to check the flesh: it should be thick, white, and firm, not yellow or slimy. If you're buying in bulk, inspect at least 10% of the lot. Local varieties like the West African Tall or the Malayan Dwarf are common; the Tall produces larger nuts with more oil. During the dry season, coconuts may be smaller but still good. Never buy coconuts that have been stored in direct sun for weeksâthey develop rancid oil. A simple test: press a piece of the flesh; if oil comes out easily, it's ready for processing. For shea nuts, quality is different: look for nuts that are smooth, brown, and without holes. But for this lesson, focus on coconuts. In Ghana, Nigeria, and CÃ´te d'Ivoire, you can find coconuts at roadside stalls, farms, or larger markets like Makola in Accra. Build a relationship with a farmer who can supply consistently. Always check the water: fresh coconuts have clear, sweet water; if it's cloudy or smells fermented, reject. Remember, good oil starts with good raw material. Spend time selecting, and you'll save money and time later.

lessons.title: Where to Buy Shea Nuts in West Africa
lessons.body: Shea nuts come from the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the Sahel belt from Senegal to Sudan. The main producing countries are Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana, Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and CÃ´te d'Ivoire. The best time to buy is during harvest season, from June to September, when nuts are plentiful and cheap. You can buy directly from village women's cooperatives, which are common in northern Ghana, Burkina Faso, and Mali. These cooperatives sell raw, unprocessed nuts in bulk. For example, in Tamale, Ghana, you can buy a 50 kg bag for around 200-300 Ghana cedis (about $20-30) during peak season. In Burkina Faso, the price is similar. If you're not near a village, go to larger markets like Bamako's MarchÃ© de Medina Coura or Ouagadougou's Rood Woko market. There, wholesalers sell shea nuts by the sack. Always inspect before buying: nuts should be smooth, brown, and free of holes (which indicate insect damage). Avoid nuts that are cracked, moldy, or smell rancid. You can also buy from aggregators who collect from many villages, but their prices are higher. For consistent quality, visit the same cooperative each season. Many cooperatives are certified organic, which can fetch a better price for your oil. If you're in Nigeria, shea nuts are abundant in Niger, Kwara, and Oyo states. In CÃ´te d'Ivoire, the northern region around Korhogo is a hub. Transportation costs matter: buying closer to home reduces spoilage and cost. Always ask for a sample and test by cracking a few nuts: the kernel should be white or cream, not discolored. If you plan to produce oil, you'll need about 2-3 kg of nuts to make 1 liter of oil. So for a small batch of 10 liters, buy 25 kg. During off-season, prices can double, so stock up during harvest. Store nuts in a dry, cool place. Building a direct relationship with a cooperative ensures a steady supply and better prices.

lessons.title: How to Negotiate with Local Farmers
lessons.body: Negotiating with farmers is about respect and fairness, not just getting the lowest price. Start by visiting the farm or market early in the morning when farmers are fresh. Introduce yourself and explain your need: you want to buy regularly, not just once. Ask about their production: how many coconuts or shea nuts they harvest per season, and what price they usually get. Listen more than you talk. In many African markets, the first price is inflated; for example, a farmer might ask 500 CFA per kg of shea nuts, but the real price is 300 CFA. Don't immediately counterâask questions about quality and quantity. If you buy in bulk (e.g., 100 kg or more), ask for a discount. A common tactic is to offer a price slightly below their asking price, but not insultingly low. For coconuts, if the market price is 200 naira per nut, offer 150 naira for a bulk purchase of 100 nuts. Be prepared to walk away if the price is too highâbut do so politely. Farmers appreciate buyers who pay cash on the spot. If you can, pay a small deposit to secure a future harvest. Also, consider offering non-cash benefits: help with transportation, or bring a gift like kola nuts or cold drinks. In shea cooperatives, prices are often fixed, but you can negotiate on volume. Always confirm the weight and quality before agreeing. Use a scale if possible; many farmers sell by volume (e.g., a tin cup) which can vary. Bring your own scale to check. If you're buying from a middleman, expect higher prices. Build trust by returning season after season. A good relationship means you get first pick and better prices. Never argue or raise your voiceâword travels fast. A fair deal today means a reliable supplier tomorrow.

lessons.title: Transporting Raw Materials Without Spoilage
lessons.body: Transporting coconuts and shea nuts requires care to prevent spoilage, especially in hot, humid African climates. For coconuts, harvest them when mature but not overripe. If you're moving them from farm to processing site, use ventilated crates or baskets, not plastic bags. Stack them no more than three layers high to avoid crushing. Coconuts can be transported in open trucks, but cover them with a tarpaulin to protect from direct sun and rain. If the journey is more than a day, keep them in a shaded, cool area overnight. Avoid piling them in a closed vehicleâheat builds up and causes mold. For shea nuts, they are more delicate. After harvest, farmers usually boil and dry the nuts, but if you buy fresh nuts, you must dry them before transport. Fresh shea nuts have high moisture and will rot in 2-3 days if not dried. Dry them in the sun for 5-7 days until the shells are hard and the kernels rattle. Then pack them in jute sacks, not plastic, to allow air circulation. Each sack should weigh about 50 kg for easy handling. During transport, stack sacks on wooden pallets to keep them off the ground. If using a truck, ensure the bed is clean and dry. Avoid mixing with strong-smelling goods like petrol or fish. For long distances, consider using a refrigerated truck only if you have large quantities; otherwise, transport at night when it's cooler. In West Africa, many roads are rough, so secure the load with ropes to prevent shifting. If you're transporting both coconuts and shea nuts, keep them separate. Coconuts can be stored for weeks if kept dry, but shea nuts need immediate processing after drying. Plan your transport to minimize time: from farm to storage should be less than 48 hours. Always check for pests: weevils can infest shea nuts. If you see holes, reject that batch. A simple rule: dry, cool, and ventilated is the key to spoilage-free transport.

lessons.title: Storage of Coconuts and Shea Nuts
lessons.body: Proper storage is critical to maintain oil quality. For coconuts, store them in a cool, dry, well-ventilated room. Ideal temperature is 20-25Â°C, with humidity below 70%. Do not store on bare ground; use wooden pallets or shelves. Arrange coconuts in a single layer or in mesh bags to allow air flow. If stacked, keep the pile below 1 meter high. Whole coconuts can last 2-3 months if stored correctly. Check weekly for mold or soft spots; remove any bad ones immediately. For longer storage, you can remove the husk and store the nuts in a dry place, but they dry out faster. In coastal areas, avoid storing near the seaâsalt air speeds spoilage. For shea nuts, storage is more demanding. After drying, shea nuts can be stored for 6-12 months if kept dry and cool. Use jute sacks and stack them on pallets in a dark room. Humidity must be below 60%; if it's higher, nuts absorb moisture and grow mold. A simple test: bite a nut; if it's soft, it's not dry enough. You can also use silica gel packets in storage rooms to absorb moisture, but that's expensive. In villages, many store shea nuts in traditional granaries with mud walls and thatched roofs, which work well. Never store shea nuts in plastic bagsâthey sweat and rot. Also, protect from rodents and insects. Use traps or natural repellents like neem leaves. If you're storing for months, inspect every two weeks. For both crops, keep them away from strong odors (e.g., kerosene, onions) because they absorb smells. If you plan to process oil, use older coconuts first. For shea, the nuts can be stored as whole nuts or cracked kernels; kernels store longer but are more prone to insect attack. Always label your storage with the date of harvest. A well-ventilated, dry store can mean the difference between high-quality oil and rancid waste.

lessons.title: Building Relationships with Suppliers
lessons.body: Building strong relationships with suppliers is the backbone of a successful oil business. Start by identifying reliable farmers or cooperatives in your area. Visit them in person, not just by phone. Show genuine interest in their work: ask about their challenges, their harvest, and their family. In many African cultures, relationship comes before business. Bring a small gift on your first visitâa bag of rice, a bottle of oil, or kola nuts. This shows respect. Be consistent: if you promise to buy 100 kg of shea nuts in June, show up in June with cash. Never make promises you can't keep. Pay fairly and on time. If you can, pay a premium for high qualityâthis encourages farmers to improve. For example, if the market price is 300 CFA per kg, offer 320 CFA for nuts with less than 5% defects. This builds loyalty. Also, consider offering advance payment or a loan for inputs like sacks or transportation. In return, ask for a commitment to sell to you first. Keep records: write down the farmer's name, location, quantity, and price. Use a simple notebook or phone app. Follow up after harvest to thank them. If a farmer has a problem, help solve itâmaybe connect them to a better market or provide storage advice. Over time, you can negotiate better prices because of trust. Join local farmer groups or cooperatives; they often have regular meetings where you can network. In West Africa, many shea cooperatives are women-led; supporting them empowers communities and improves your reputation. Avoid middlemen who add cost without value. Instead, buy directly. If you're in a city, travel to rural areas at least twice a year. Remember, a good supplier will prioritize you during scarce times. They might even save the best nuts for you. Building relationships takes time, but it pays off in consistent quality and supply. Treat your suppliers as partners, not just sellers.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a fresh coconut?
options: A) It is light for its size
B) It has a dry, brown husk with no cracks
C) It has a sour smell
quiz.explanation: A fresh coconut has a dry, brown husk and no cracks, and should feel heavy.

quiz.q: How much oil can you expect from 2-3 kg of shea nuts?
quiz.explanation: On average, 2-3 kg of shea nuts yield about 1 liter of oil.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy shea nuts in West Africa?
quiz.explanation: Shea nuts are harvested from June to September, so prices are lowest then.

quiz.q: What should you avoid when transporting coconuts?
options: B) Stacking them more than three layers high
D) Keeping them in a shaded area
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than three layers high can crush the coconuts at the bottom.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for coconuts?
quiz.explanation: Coconuts store best at 20-25Â°C with low humidity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice when negotiating with farmers?
options: A) Start with a very low offer
B) Pay cash on the spot
C) Argue loudly to get a better price
D) Avoid asking about their production
quiz.explanation: Paying cash on the spot is appreciated and builds trust.

quiz.q: How long can dried shea nuts be stored under good conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dried shea nuts can last 6-12 months if kept dry and cool.

quiz.q: What is a common test to check if shea nuts are dry enough for storage?
options: A) Shake them and listen for a rattle
B) Bite one; it should be hard
C) Smell them for a rancid odor
D) Drop them in water; they should float
quiz.explanation: If a nut is soft when bitten, it still has too much moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you not store shea nuts in plastic bags?
quiz.explanation: Plastic bags trap moisture, causing shea nuts to sweat and rot.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of building a relationship with a supplier?
options: A) You can pay less than market price
B) You get first pick and consistent supply
C) You can avoid paying taxes
D) You don't need to inspect quality
quiz.explanation: Good relationships lead to priority access and reliable supply.

quiz.q: Which region is a major hub for shea nuts in CÃ´te d'Ivoire?
quiz.explanation: Korhogo in northern CÃ´te d'Ivoire is a major shea nut hub.

quiz.q: What should you do before transporting fresh shea nuts?
options: B) Dry them in the sun for 5-7 days
C) Store them in plastic bags
quiz.explanation: Fresh shea nuts must be dried to prevent rot during transport.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor-quality coconuts?
quiz.explanation: Mold or soft spots indicate spoilage.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect stored coconuts?
quiz.explanation: Weekly inspection helps catch mold or spoilage early.

quiz.q: What is a good way to negotiate a bulk discount?
options: A) Demand a lower price immediately
B) Offer a price slightly below asking but not insulting
C) Walk away without a word
quiz.explanation: A reasonable counteroffer shows you are serious but fair.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use a scale when buying shea nuts?
options: A) To check the weight accurately
C) To avoid paying too much
quiz.explanation: Using a scale ensures you pay for the actual weight, avoiding overpayment.

quiz.q: What is a traditional storage method for shea nuts in villages?
options: B) Mud granaries with thatched roofs
quiz.explanation: Mud granaries with thatched roofs provide cool, dry storage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see holes in shea nuts?
options: A) Buy them at a discount
quiz.explanation: Holes indicate insect damage, which can spread and reduce quality.

quiz.q: How can you protect stored shea nuts from rodents?
options: A) Use traps or neem leaves
quiz.explanation: Traps and natural repellents like neem leaves deter rodents.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying directly from a cooperative?
options: B) Consistent quality and better prices
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives often offer consistent quality and fair prices.

quiz.q: What should you bring on your first visit to a farmer?
options: B) A small gift like kola nuts
quiz.explanation: A small gift shows respect and helps build rapport.

quiz.q: How long can whole coconuts last if stored properly?
quiz.explanation: Whole coconuts can last 2-3 months in cool, dry conditions.

quiz.q: What is a sign that shea nuts are not dry enough for storage?
options: B) They are soft when bitten
C) They are hard and brown
quiz.explanation: Softness indicates high moisture content, which leads to mold.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing coconuts near the sea?
quiz.explanation: Salt air increases humidity and speeds spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when transporting shea nuts?
options: A) Stack sacks on wooden pallets
D) Leave them in the sun
quiz.explanation: Wooden pallets keep sacks off the ground and allow air circulation.

quiz.q: What should you do if a farmer offers you a price above market?
options: B) Politely negotiate or walk away
quiz.explanation: Politely negotiating or walking away is respectful and effective.

quiz.q: What is a key factor in building long-term supplier relationships?
quiz.explanation: Consistency and fairness build trust and loyalty.

quiz.q: How many layers of coconuts should you stack during transport?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 3 layers can crush the bottom coconuts.

quiz.q: What is a common pest that affects stored shea nuts?
quiz.explanation: Weevils can infest shea nuts, causing damage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label storage with harvest date?
options: A) To know which batch to use first
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps you use older stock first, reducing spoilage.
